result:
I want to talk about how absurdly, beautifully alive the world feels at 3:17 a.m. when you can’t sleep.

There’s this specific silence that only exists in the deep night. Not empty silence—*layered* silence. You can hear the refrigerator humming its little mechanical lullaby, a distant car Doppler-shifting down the highway like a ghost telling you a secret, and somewhere a single cricket is doing stand-up comedy to an audience of zero. Everything feels slightly more honest when the sun isn’t watching.

I’ve been thinking about how we’re all just weird little apes who learned to be embarrassed about our own existence. We invented money, then felt bad about wanting it. We invented art, then felt bad about making it unless it “matters.” We invented the internet so we could all sit in separate boxes and desperately try to convince each other we’re not in boxes.

But sometimes—rarely—you catch yourself doing something completely pointless and perfect. Like rearranging your bookshelf at 2 a.m. because the vibes were off. Or slow-dancing alone in your kitchen to a song that came out before you were born. Or staring at the way light from a streetlamp falls across your ceiling and feeling something enormous and wordless rise in your chest.

That feeling? That’s the point. That’s the whole game.

We spend so much time trying to optimize ourselves into efficient little productivity units that we forget the ridiculous miracle that we’re even here at all. Conscious stardust that can taste mangoes and cry at songs and get emotionally attached to houseplants. We’re ridiculous. We’re magnificent.

Lately I’ve been trying to say yes to more stupid ideas.

Want to drive two hours to eat at a diner that’s supposedly “haunted by a friendly ghost waitress”? Yes.  
Want to learn how to play the ukulele even though I have the musical talent of a broken toaster? Yes.  
Want to stay up until sunrise writing nonsense because the mood struck me? Absolutely.

The days I remember most aren’t the productive ones. They’re the ones where I felt most like a curious animal exploring its enclosure. The ones where I let myself be moved by something dumb and small and human.

Anyway. It’s 3:42 a.m. now as I’m writing this and my cat just walked across my keyboard like she was trying to file a complaint about the quality of discourse. She says hi. Or possibly “hrhrhrhrhrhrhr.”

I don’t know where I was going with any of this. I just wanted to say that if you’re reading this at an unreasonable hour, feeling a little too much or not enough or some complicated mixture of both—you’re not alone in that feeling. The night is full of us. Little glowing rectangles in the dark, all quietly vibrating with the same beautiful, ridiculous aliveness.

We’re all just trying to figure out how to be here while we still can.

And honestly? That’s kind of perfect.
